argument: Hegel is responding to Kant's split between the world as we experience it and an unreachable world of "things in themselves," and he questions why we need to assume that hidden real world exists at all. To make his case he works through the theories of knowledge that came before him, showing that neither sense-certainty (knowledge from immediate sensation) nor perception (knowledge from organizing sensations into objects) can stand on their own as a self-sufficient basis for knowledge, since both always turn out to depend on something outside themselves.
keyIdeas: Leibniz and Hume left only two kinds of knowable statements, truths of reason and truths of fact, which seemed to reduce philosophy to either word-analysis or empirical verification, jobs scientists already do.

Kant answered this by proposing synthetic a priori propositions and the idea that philosophy could study the mental lens through which we experience the world, distinguishing that experience from an inaccessible world of things in themselves.
Hegel questions the need to assume this hidden 'real' world behind our experience at all, wondering whether consciousness and its relations to itself might be all there is.
Sense-certainty only ever gives 'truth of has-been' rather than 'truth of being,' since sensed objects (illustrated by nighttime) are constantly changing and stop being true almost immediately.

Perception, illustrated by the saltshaker, fails to be self-sufficient too: calling the salt white or bitter only makes sense by comparison to everything else you've experienced, and even the boundary of 'the thing' (the glass canister) is an arbitrary line we impose.

Leibniz's category of statements verifiable through immediate empirical experiment.
Kant's proposed third type of proposition, beyond truths of reason and fact, that let philosophy study the mind's lens on experience.
The mode of consciousness that tries to ground knowledge in immediate sensory experience.
Universals are shared qualities like redness; particulars are the individual objects that possess those qualities.
The mode of consciousness that organizes sense-objects by finding relationships between them, e.g. comparing the salt to everything else you've sensed.
